55:## Performance vs pyMUSIC
- IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above
  Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins.
- Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins;
  select the bins that carry signal energy.

## Performance vs pyMUSIC

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/benchmark-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Bar chart of time per call on a linear scale; every bar except pyMUSIC's IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins is only a few pixels wide or less, and value labels give the numbers. musicrs is 28× faster than pyMUSIC for narrowband DOA on a 1 s recording, 14× on a 2 s recording, 191× and 122× for single-bin IFB-MUSIC, and 784× for IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins (11.5 s vs 14.7 ms)." src="docs/benchmark.svg">
</picture>

The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the
result, with pyMUSIC run unmodified. musicrs is **14× to 784× faster** by mean time per call.
pyMUSIC spends ~140 ms per pseudo-spectrum building 720 `float128` steering vectors in a
Python loop, whatever the recording length, so the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC (one spectrum
per bin) and narrows for longer recordings, where musicrs's own work (Hilbert transform,
covariance) grows with the sample count.

| Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Narrowband DOA · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 159 ms ± 8.03 ms | 158 ms | 150 ms – 173 ms | 5.0% |  |
|  | musicrs | 1000 | 5.63 ms ± 570 µs | 5.41 ms | 5.1 ms – 6.73 ms | 10.1% | 28× |
| Narrowband DOA · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 163 ms ± 18.9 ms | 157 ms | 151 ms – 205 ms | 11.6% |  |
|  | musicrs | 1000 | 11.7 ms ± 832 µs | 11.5 ms | 11 ms – 13.7 ms | 7.1% | 14× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 144 ms ± 7.19 ms | 142 ms | 139 ms – 157 ms | 5.0% |  |
|  | musicrs | 1000 | 757 µs ± 121 µs | 770 µs | 633 µs – 845 µs | 16.0% | 191× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 152 ms ± 6.85 ms | 151 ms | 143 ms – 164 ms | 4.5% |  |
|  | musicrs | 1000 | 1.24 ms ± 94 µs | 1.22 ms | 1.15 ms – 1.44 ms | 7.5% | 122× |
| IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 30 | 11.53 s ± 244 ms | 11.43 s | 11.30 s – 11.83 s | 2.1% |  |
|  | musicrs | 1000 | 14.7 ms ± 748 µs | 14.5 ms | 13.9 ms – 16.4 ms | 5.1% | 784× |

Every call is timed separately (pyMUSIC: 200 calls per case, 30 for 80 bins; musicrs: 1000)
after 3 warm-up calls. Machine: Intel N150 (3 cores), Linux, `performance` governor, rustc
1.88, Python 3.10 / numpy 1.23.5; see [`bench/`](bench/README.md) for the harnesses and how to
reproduce, and [`bench/results/`](bench/results/) for the raw samples.

### Distribution of the timings

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/benchmark-distribution-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Histograms of time per call divided by the median, one per workload and implementation. All are right-skewed: a sharp peak near the fastest calls and a tail of slower calls. musicrs IFB-MUSIC with one bin on the 1 s recording has two clusters, around 0.85 and 1.05 times the median." src="docs/benchmark-distribution.svg">
</picture>

- **Not normal.** Shapiro-Wilk rejects normality for every case (p < 0.001), on t and on
  log t. Every distribution is right-skewed (skew 1.1 to 3.2, and 16.6 for one case with a
  single 5× outlier): a sharp edge near the fastest call and a tail of slower ones, the shape
  of interference that can only add time. A log-normal fits better than a normal in every
  case, but none is log-normal either.
- **Scheduling moves the mean by a few percent.** The mean is at most 4.2 % above the median,
  and the outliers (calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas) raise the mean by at most
  3.8 % (*tail excess*). Mean and median give the same speedups to within a few percent.
  Because the distributions are skewed, ± stddev overstates the spread below the mean; the
  p5 – p95 column shows the real range.
- **Slow calls come in runs.** Lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.3 to 0.7, so neighbouring calls are
  alike. Isolated preemptions would hit calls independently; runs point to slower changes in
  machine state (CPU frequency, caches, the core the process runs on). It is clearest for
  musicrs IFB-MUSIC with one bin on the 1 s recording: two clusters, ~650 µs and ~790 µs. A
  re-run reproduced both clusters, in a different order.
- **Run to run**, a second musicrs run gave means 3 to 8 % different. Read the numbers as
  about ± 10 %; the speedups are far larger than that.

# musicrs Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)?; // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))?; ``` Bad input (wrong channel count, NaN, silence, too many sources, an unusable angle grid, …) is returned as a `MusicError`. For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, with pyMUSIC run unmodified. musicrs is **14× to 784× faster** by mean time per call. pyMUSIC spends ~140 ms per pseudo-spectrum building 720 `float128` steering vectors in a Python loop, whatever the recording length, so the gap is widest for IFB-MUSIC (one spectrum per bin) and narrows for longer recordings, where musicrs's own work (Hilbert transform, covariance) grows with the sample count. | Workload | Implementation | n | Mean ± stddev | Median | p5 – p95 | CV | Speedup (mean) | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Narrowband DOA · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 159 ms ± 8.03 ms | 158 ms | 150 ms – 173 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 5.63 ms ± 570 µs | 5.41 ms | 5.1 ms – 6.73 ms | 10.1% | 28× | | Narrowband DOA · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 163 ms ± 18.9 ms | 157 ms | 151 ms – 205 ms | 11.6% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 11.7 ms ± 832 µs | 11.5 ms | 11 ms – 13.7 ms | 7.1% | 14× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 144 ms ± 7.19 ms | 142 ms | 139 ms – 157 ms | 5.0% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 757 µs ± 121 µs | 770 µs | 633 µs – 845 µs | 16.0% | 191× | | IFB-MUSIC, 1 bin · 2 s recording | pyMUSIC | 200 | 152 ms ± 6.85 ms | 151 ms | 143 ms – 164 ms | 4.5% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 1.24 ms ± 94 µs | 1.22 ms | 1.15 ms – 1.44 ms | 7.5% | 122× | | IFB-MUSIC, 80 bins · 1 s recording | pyMUSIC | 30 | 11.53 s ± 244 ms | 11.43 s | 11.30 s – 11.83 s | 2.1% | | | | musicrs | 1000 | 14.7 ms ± 748 µs | 14.5 ms | 13.9 ms – 16.4 ms | 5.1% | 784× | Every call is timed separately (pyMUSIC: 200 calls per case, 30 for 80 bins; `# Runtime benchmark: musicrs vs pyMUSIC and numpy

Times three implementations of the same algorithm on the same calls and recordings, keeps
every timed call, and summarises the distributions. The results and charts are in the
top-level README, section *Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy*.

- **pyMUSIC**: the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), unmodified
  (\`bench_pymusic.py\`).
- **numpy (vectorized)**: pyMUSIC's algorithm written idiomatically in numpy
  (\`bench_numpy.py\`). pyMUSIC spends almost all of its time in a Python loop that builds every
  steering vector element by element in \`float128\` with \`np.matrix\`, so on its own it
  measures how pyMUSIC is written, not what Python can do. This one keeps the same analytic
  signal, \`np.linalg.eig\`, eigenvector order, steering vectors and peak, but works in
  \`float64\` and builds the steering vectors of all angles in one array operation each call
  (nothing is cached between calls). It runs on one BLAS thread, as musicrs runs on one
  thread. Before timing each case, it checks its result against pyMUSIC's on the same
  recording (spectrum within a relative 1e-6, same peak up to the θ / 2π − θ ambiguity of the
  linear array) and stops if they differ.
- **musicrs** (\`examples/bench_pymusic.rs\`).`);

`| Workload | pyMUSIC | numpy (\`bench_numpy.py\`) | musicrs | Recordings |
|---|---|---|---|---|

brep(`Both harnesses make 3 untimed warm-up calls, then time every call on its own

`All harnesses make 3 untimed warm-up calls, then time every call on its own

# Runtime benchmark: musicrs vs pyMUSIC

Times the original [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC) and musicrs on the
same calls and recordings, keeps every timed call, and summarises the distributions. The
results and charts are in the top-level README, section *Performance vs pyMUSIC*.

## Workloads

All use the 1400 Hz / 40° recordings in `tests/data/single-source/` (4 channels, 16 kHz)
and the default estimator (Kinect array, 720 angles over [0, 2π)).

| Workload | pyMUSIC | musicrs | Recordings |
|---|---|---|---|
| `narrowband` | `MUSICEst.getSourceAngles(data, 1, 1400)` | `estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)` | 1 s, 2 s |
| `ifb_one_bin` | `IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=[14])` | `ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))` | 1 s, 2 s |
| `ifb_all_bins` | `IFBMUSICSpectrum(data, pos, 160, bins=range(1, 81))` | `ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&(1..=80)))` | 1 s |

Each call includes everything from the real-valued samples to the result: analytic signal
or STFT, covariance, eigendecomposition and the spectrum. Reading the WAV file is not timed.
`ifb_all_bins` lists the 80 non-DC bins explicitly because pyMUSIC's `bins=None` would also
include DC and musicrs's would not. It runs on the 1 s recording only: one pyMUSIC call
takes about 11 s, and the cost is the 720-angle spectrum per bin, not the recording length.

Both harnesses make 3 untimed warm-up calls, then time every call on its own
(`time.perf_counter_ns` / `std::time::Instant`) and write it to a CSV. pyMUSIC gets 200
samples per case (30 for `ifb_all_bins`), musicrs 1000. pyMUSIC runs unmodified with
`np.linalg.eig`; the only shim is the Python-2 index fix in pySoundToolbox, as in
`tests/golden/generate_golden.py`.

## Statistics

`analyze.py` reports mean ± stddev and the median for every case, and investigates the
shape of the distribution, because scheduling noise (preemption, interrupts, frequency
changes) only ever adds time and so appears as a right tail rather than as symmetric
spread:

- spread: MAD, p5/p95, min/max, coefficient of variation (stddev / mean);
- shape: skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk tests on t and on log t, and whether a
  normal or a log-normal fit has the lower AIC;
- outliers: calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas (1.4826 · MAD), their share, and the
  *tail excess*, how much they raise the mean over the mean of the other calls.

A small gap between mean and median and a small tail excess mean scheduling has little
influence on the result; the median is then a fair single number, and the mean ± stddev
an honest one.

## Reproduce

Run the two benchmarks one after the other on an otherwise idle machine, so they do not
compete for cores:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC /path/to/pyMUSIC
git clone https://github.com/Trion/pySoundToolbox /path/to/pySoundToolbox

cargo run --release --example bench_pymusic -- bench/results/musicrs.csv      # ~1 min
uv run --python 3.10 --with 'numpy==1.23.5' python -I bench/bench_pymusic.py \
    /path/to/pyMUSIC /path/to/pySoundToolbox bench/results/pymusic.csv        # ~10 min
uv run --python 3.12 --with numpy --with scipy --with matplotlib \
    python -I bench/analyze.py
```

`BENCH_SCALE=0.1` scales every sample count down for a quick check (both harnesses).
`analyze.py` writes `bench/results/summary.{csv,md}` and the charts in `docs/`.
`bench/results/environment.txt` records the machine the committed results come from.

# CLAUDE.md

## Project Overview

**musicrs** is a Rust port of the MUSIC (MUltiple SIgnal Classification) algorithm for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone/antenna arrays. Based on R. O. Schmidt's 1986 algorithm and the Python pyMUSIC implementation.

## Commands

```bash
# Build
cargo build
cargo build --release

# Test
cargo test              # all tests except slow ones (#[ignore = "slow"])
cargo test -- --include-ignored   # full suite, including slow tests (CI runs this)
cargo test --lib        # unit tests only
cargo test --test '*'   # integration tests only
cargo test --test golden_test   # parity with the original pyMUSIC spectra
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings   # CI runs this and `cargo fmt --check`
cargo audit             # RustSec advisories in Cargo.lock (CI runs this; install cargo-audit first)

# Documentation
cargo doc --open
```

## Architecture

```
src/
├── lib.rs      # Public API exports and crate-level docs
├── error.rs    # MusicError (returned by every fallible public function) and `musicrs::error::Result` (not re-exported at the root)
├── music.rs    # Core MUSIC algorithm (MusicEstimator, spectrum, DOA estimation)
└── stft.rs     # Signal processing (STFT, analytic signal via Hilbert transform)
tests/
├── common/mod.rs                # Shared WAV/filename/angle helpers, ErrorLog
├── integration_test.rs          # Narrowband DOA on every WAV recording (±0.5°)
├── ifb_test.rs                  # IFB-MUSIC on the tone's bin (nfft 160), below Nyquist (±0.5°); repeated and reordered bins
├── errors_test.rs               # Every MusicError the public API returns
├── golden_test.rs               # Spectra vs. pyMUSIC (incl. partial interval, 2 sources narrowband and IFB, nfft 320/1024); analytic signal vs. scipy; musicrs snapshots at/above Nyquist
├── broadband_test.rs            # IFB-MUSIC on composite multi-tone signals; two sources at different angles
├── noisy_data_test.rs           # Narrowband and IFB (energy-selected bins) DOA with added white noise
├── synthetic_test.rs            # Synthetic plane waves: 2-D arrays, 2–3 sources, coherent sources (not resolved), endfire, edge cases, 48 kHz
├── golden/                      # pyMUSIC reference CSVs, *.musicrs.csv snapshots, generate_golden.py
└── data/single-source/*.wav     # 4-channel 24-bit 16kHz test recordings
examples/bench_pymusic.rs        # musicrs side of the runtime benchmark vs pyMUSIC
bench/                           # pyMUSIC harness, analyze.py (stats + charts), results/; see bench/README.md
docs/benchmark*.svg              # charts shown in the README (light and dark), generated by bench/analyze.py
```

**Key types:**
- `MusicEstimator` — main struct; configure antenna positions, angle search range/step, sample rate, and number of sources
- `MusicEstimator::estimate_doa_from_real()` — real-data entry point (removes each channel's mean, analytic signal per channel, then `estimate_doa`), like pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles`
- `MusicEstimator::ifb_music_spectrum()` — wideband variant; bin frequencies use the estimator's `sample_rate`, so tones above Nyquist cannot be recovered
- `select_bins_by_energy()` — picks the IFB bins within N dB of the strongest; with `bins = None` noise-only bins dominate the geometric mean
- `analytic_signal()` — converts real signal to complex via Hilbert transform (FFT-based)
- `stft()` — Short-Time Fourier Transform with configurable window and overlap

- `MusicError` — bad data (wrong row count or covariance shape, no samples, NaN/inf, silence) and bad parameters (too many or zero sources, angle grid incl. spans over 2π, frequency ≤ 0 or non-finite, sample rate, antenna positions, `nfft`, overlap, threshold, no usable bins) are returned as `Err`; the public API does not panic on them and does not return a quiet wrong answer. The estimator's fields are checked where they are used, not in `new()`, because the fields are public. `noise_subspace` reads only the lower triangle of `cov`; IFB never uses the DC bin

**Core algorithm flow:**
1. Compute covariance matrix of complex multichannel input
2. Hermitian eigendecomposition (`faer`) → signal/noise subspace split
3. Compute MUSIC pseudo-spectrum using steering vectors
4. Peak detection → DOA estimates in radians

## Dependencies

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `nalgebra` | Matrix types and linear algebra |
| `num-complex` | Complex number arithmetic |
| `rustfft` | FFT for STFT and Hilbert transform |
| `faer` | Numerically stable Hermitian eigendecomposition |
| `hound` (dev) | Reading WAV test fixtures |
| `approx` (dev) | Floating-point approximate equality in tests |

## Testing

Integration tests load WAV files from `tests/data/single-source/` and compare DOA estimates with the ground truth in the file name. Clean recordings land exactly on the true angle, so their tolerance is one 0.5° grid step; noisy and broadband-triple tests use tolerances set a little above the measured worst error. `common::ErrorLog` prints the worst error per test (`cargo test -- --nocapture`), which is the number to re-check before changing a tolerance. File naming convention:

```
single-source_<freq>Hz_<doa>deg_<duration>s.wav
```

Test data covers:
- Frequencies: 300 Hz – 9.1 kHz (in ~1.1 kHz steps)
- Angles: 0°, 40°, 80°, 120°, 160°
- Durations: 1 s and 2 s
- Array: Kinect 4-mic geometry

## Workflow

- Before implementing a non-trivial change, propose a plan and get it approved first. While planning, ask clarifying questions about anything ambiguous (scope, API shape, defaults, test data) rather than guessing.

- Make changes on a branch, never directly on `main`:
  - `feat/<feature-name>` for new features
  - `fix/<bugfix-name>` for bug fixes
- Structure work in reasonably sized commits: each commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own.
- A project Stop hook (`.claude/settings.json` → `.claude/hooks/run-tests.sh`) runs `cargo test` when a turn ends with changed code under `src/`, `tests/` or `Cargo.*`, and sends failures back to Claude. Tests that take more than ~10 s are marked `#[ignore = "slow"]`, so the hook skips them; run `cargo test -- --include-ignored` for the full suite. Set `MUSICRS_SKIP_HOOK_TESTS=1` before starting Claude Code to turn the hook off.
- Parallel builds (subagents in separate worktrees, or a second `cargo test` next to the Stop hook) must not share a Cargo target directory. Worktrees of this crate produce the same test-binary paths (e.g. `target/debug/deps/noisy_data_test-<hash>`), and cargo releases its build lock before running the tests, so one run can execute another worktree's binary: tests go missing or fail on code that isn't there, or a binary being rewritten fails with "Permission denied". Give each worktree its own `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` (on this 3-core machine also `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1`), and check that new tests appear by name in the output before trusting a run.

## Notes

- Rust edition 2024, MSRV follows current stable toolchain
- No `rustfmt.toml` or `clippy.toml` — use `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` defaults
- Golden files: `*.eigh.csv` (pyMUSIC with `np.linalg.eigh`) and `*.hilbert_n<N>.scipy.csv` (`scipy.signal.hilbert`) must match value-by-value; `*.eig.csv` (pyMUSIC as published) only by peak location, because `np.linalg.eig` returns a non-orthogonal noise basis on this near-noiseless data. Regenerate with the command in `tests/golden/generate_golden.py`.
- Snapshot files: `*.narrowband.musicrs.csv` in `tests/golden/` are musicrs's own narrowband spectra at and above Nyquist (8000 Hz, 9100 Hz), not pyMUSIC references (musicrs deliberately differs from pyMUSIC there). They pin the at/above-Nyquist steering-vector behaviour to a relative tolerance of 1e-9. After an intended change, regenerate with `MUSICRS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo test --test golden_test` and review the diff.
- Sign convention: musicrs uses a non-conjugated analytic signal with an `exp(+j2πfτ)` steering vector; pyMUSIC conjugates the analytic signal and uses `exp(−j2πfτ)`. Equivalent below Nyquist. The above-Nyquist sign flip and the real steering vector at Nyquist are musicrs additions tuned to the test data.
